summary: Discusses how mobility affects NSIS protocol operation and state management, and shows how NSIS behaves with different mobility management protocols. It is informational.

eli5.summary: What happens to reserved space on a road when your car changes route.

questions: how does nsis handle mobile handovers
how does nsis differ from rsvp for mobile nodes
subtitle: How network signaling protocols adapt when mobile devices change their connection points.

tldr.problem: Mobile devices that move between network access points experience route changes that break traditional signaling protocols, which tie signaling state to IP addresses that are changing.
tldr.mechanism: NSIS decouples signaling state from IP addresses by using a session identifier (SID) and message routing information (MRI). When routes change, NSIS updates state locally on affected path segments (crossover nodes) instead of tearing down and rebuilding everything.
tldr.outcome: NSIS protocols work well in mobile environments because state is not lost when addresses change. The SID allows signaling to survive handovers as long as any part of the path remains the same.

today: RFC 5980 is an Informational specification describing NSIS behavior in mobile environments. It has not been updated or obsoleted; the analysis and guidance it provides on mobile handovers remain the definitive reference for implementing NSIS in networks where devices move between access routers.

sections.title: NSIS and Its Two Layers
sections.content:
The NSIS protocol suite defines how networks signal the need for special handling of traffic flows. It consists of two layers: the transport layer (GIST, or General Internet Signaling Transport) and the signaling layer (NSLP, which holds application-specific protocols like QoS NSLP for quality-of-service guarantees and NAT/FW NSLP for firewall rules).

NSIS separates signaling state (the configuration being applied) from the flow identity (which packets are being affected). The flow is identified by source address, destination address, and port numbers in the Message Routing Information (MRI). When a mobile node moves and gets a new address, the signaling layer is notified that the route has changed, and it can update the state without restarting the entire session.
sections.eli5: The signaling protocol has a label (session ID) for the delivery, separate from the truck's current location. When the truck moves, only the route gets updated, not the label.

sections.title: The Nine Challenges Mobility Creates
sections.content:
When a mobile device hands over to a new access router, several problems arise. First, the device gets a new IP address, making the old routing information incorrect. Second, double state occurs: the old path still has signaling state that will not expire for seconds or minutes, wasting resources. Third, frequent handovers in mobile networks happen much faster than traditional route failures, so state timeouts must be shorter.

Fourth, the network must identify the crossover node (CRN), the point where old and new paths merge. Fifth, upstream and downstream paths are often asymmetric due to Internet routing, so each direction needs independent state update. Sixth, when a mobile node is the receiver, it cannot easily initiate upstream signaling. Seventh, state updates raise authorization questions about which entities can modify state on behalf of the moving node. Eighth, old access routers may report the mobile node as unreachable, causing false teardown of valid state. Finally, IP-in-IP tunneling used by mobility protocols hides the inner addresses, breaking packet classification for QoS reservations.
sections.eli5: When a truck moves, the old route still thinks it is coming, leftover reservations waste space, the network must figure out where paths join, and different directions need separate cleanup.

sections.title: How Crossover Nodes Localize State Updates
sections.content:
When a handover occurs and new routing information reaches a node on both the old and new paths, that node becomes a crossover node. Instead of requiring end-to-end signaling, the CRN can localize the update: it keeps the state on the common (unchanged) portion of the path and either tears down the old branch or establishes the new branch independently.

For downstream state update (sender to receiver), the mobile node initiates a new RESERVE message with a new sequence number for the new path. When this message reaches the downstream CRN, the node realizes the upstream peer has changed and begins state setup toward the receiver. The CRN then sends a notify message back to the old path to tear down state there. For upstream state update (receiver to sender), either the correspondent node initiates a refresh when it detects the mobile node has moved, or the mobile node sends a notify message upstream when it detects a route change and has GIST connectivity to the old path. The crossover node discovers these updates implicitly: when it sees the same session ID with a different peer identifier (SII-Handle), it knows it is the CRN.
sections.eli5: The junction point between old and new roads sees traffic from both routes. It keeps everything working on the unchanged main road while fixing only the changed branches.

sections.title: Working with Mobile IPv4 and IPv6
sections.content:
Mobile IPv4 adds complexity: when a mobile node receives data, packets flow through a tunnel from the home agent to the foreign agent or the node itself. NSIS must signal twice: once for the end-to-end path and once inside the tunnel. The two RESERVE operations can be preconfigured (both QoS sessions defined in advance) or dynamically created (the entry point of the tunnel creates tunnel sessions on demand).

Mobile IPv6 with route optimization is simpler: the mobile node can directly signal to the correspondent node without going through a home agent. NSIS crossover node discovery and state update work as described above. However, if tunneling occurs (because the mobile node sends data through a home agent), NSIS must manage both the tunnel and end-to-end paths separately but in coordination.

QoS NSLP must be aware of tunneling overhead: when resources are reserved, the tunnel header adds extra bytes that must be accounted for in the reservation. NAT/Firewall signaling must complete before mobility binding updates are sent, so that the firewall and NAT rules are ready for the mobility control messages themselves.
sections.eli5: When data is tunneled, the signaling needs separate reservations for the tunnel segment and the end-to-end path, and must account for the extra bytes the tunnel adds.

sections.title: Future Challenges: Multiple Interfaces and Dead Peers
sections.content:
A mobile device with multiple network interfaces can use several paths simultaneously for load balancing. NSIS must distinguish between a handover CRN (where one interface is handing over) and a load-balancing CRN (where two active interfaces have traffic on different paths). One proposed approach introduces a path classification identifier in signaling messages to let the CRN know the intent. When an intermediate node fails and becomes unreachable, the network must rediscover crossover nodes and reestablish state quickly. These scenarios are identified as needing further study.

The RFC also notes that NSIS could benefit from tighter integration with other mobility protocols like Hierarchical Mobile IPv6 and Seamoby protocols to reduce signaling latency during interdomain handovers. Currently, only basic mobile IP scenarios are fully specified.
sections.eli5: Future problems include telling apart normal load balancing from emergency handovers when multiple routes are active, and recovering quickly if intermediate nodes break.
